definition: Emergency calls received on a standard 10-digit phone line rather than through the 9-1-1 network.
The three-digit number for the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline in the United States and Canada.
Automatic Call Distributor. A telephony system that distributes incoming calls to available agents based on predefined rules.
Association of Public Safety Communications Officials.
A PSAP or dispatch center that assumes call-taking or dispatch responsibilities when another center is unavailable or overwhelmed.
The 60-minute period with the highest call volume in a given day or period. Used for capacity planning.
Computer-Aided Dispatch. Systems used by dispatchers to track status and location of resources.
The interval from when a call is answered until it is dispatched, or until the call is dispatchable â€” that is, until the telecommunicator has enough information to dispatch it.
Commission on Fire Accreditation International.
A call transfer where the transferring telecommunicator disconnects once the call is routed, without confirming the receiving party has answered.
The number of calls being handled simultaneously at a given moment. A key driver of NG9-1-1 system capacity and cost.
The total hours a telecommunicator is scheduled to work in a year, per their employment agreement.
Full-Time Equivalent. A unit that indicates the workload of an employed person.
International Academies of Emergency Dispatch.
A real-world occurrence, or event, for which one or more calls may be received.
An agreement between agencies or jurisdictions to provide assistance and resources during emergencies.
National Crime Information Center. The FBI's criminal justice information system, used by PSAPs for warrant checks, stolen vehicle lookups, and other law-enforcement queries.
National Emergency Number Association.
Contracted hours minus vacation, training, sick leave, and other non-operational time. Represents actual time available for call handling.
Next Generation 9-1-1. An initiative to update the 9-1-1 service infrastructure to improve public emergency communications services in a wireless mobile society.
Next Generation Core Services. The IP-based infrastructure that routes 9-1-1 calls in an NG9-1-1 environment.
Public Safety Answering Point. A facility equipped and staffed to receive 9-1-1 calls.
Quality Assurance.
Quality Improvement.
A transmission on a radio channel, typically initiated by pressing the push-to-talk button. Counted as a workload unit in dispatch operations.
Request for Assistance. A request from one agency to another for support or resources.
Real-Time Text. A text-based communication method that transmits characters as they are typed, used for accessibility.
Emergency messaging via satellite, available on certain mobile devices when cellular service is unavailable.
Service Level Agreement. A commitment between a service provider and a client.
Teletypewriter / Telecommunications Device for the Deaf.
A call transfer where the transferring telecommunicator remains on the line until the receiving party answers and the handoff is complete.
The number of hours in a standard work year used for FTE calculations. Common conventions are 2,080 hours (5 x 8-hour shifts) and 2,184 hours (12-hour / "Pittman" schedule).
Post-call work performed by the telecommunicator after the call ends, before they are available for the next call. May include documentation, follow-up calls, or system updates.
